headline: Legacy media under sustained pressure from streaming and social media; Fox, Disney, Paramount, Comcast all flat or down while market is up 14-15%
reasoning: Streaming platforms like YouTube and Amazon Prime are taking viewership from legacy broadcast and cable. Streaming services like Disney+, Paramount+ and Peacock are less profitable than the legacy channels they replace due to high content and distribution spending. Consumers now spend over 90 minutes a day on social networks, displacing TV viewing. Since the 'Winter of Discontent' publication, Netflix, Paramount, Fox, Disney, and Comcast are flat or down while the market is up 14-15%. Only Warner Brothers is up on a takeover offer.
quote: Streaming platforms are taped like YouTube and Amazon Prime are taking viewership away from the legacy broadcast and cable companies. Streaming companies like Disney Plus and Paramount Plus and Peacock are less profitable for their parent companies than the cable and broadcast channels they're replacing... consumers and viewers now spend more than 90 minutes a day on social networks. And that's displacing time used to be spent watching television... Netflix is down. So is Paramount. So is Fox and Disney and Comcast are flat at a time when the markets up, you know, 14, 15 percent.

headline: Hyperscalers have underperformed the tech sector and S&P this year; falling free cash flow, rising debt and absence of ROIC proof were the warning signs
reasoning: In January 2026, the call highlighted risks from falling free cash flow, rising reliance on debt to fund capex, declining stock buybacks, and insufficient evidence of positive returns on invested capital. Since then, hyperscalers have underperformed the tech sector, the broad market, and the S&P ex-Technology. Revaluation gains on Anthropic/OpenAI positions inflated reported Q2 earnings significantly, masking weaker underlying performance.
quote: The next one that worked out was a comment that we had in the outlook this year on the end of the outperformance of the hyperscaler stocks. In January, we were really focused on the risks in terms of falling free cash flow, rising reliance on debt to fund capital spending, a decline in stock buybacks, and not enough signs of positive returns on invested capital. And so far, the hyperscalers this year have underperformed the tech sector, the broad market, and the S&P, X-Technology.

headline: Stock has plummeted and credit default swap spreads surged from 30-50bps to over 200bps; $60bn OpenAI contract was revenue that didn't exist yet, for infrastructure not yet built, funded by debt at 500% debt/equity
reasoning: Oracle jumped 25% after being promised $60bn/year from OpenAI, but that is revenue OpenAI doesn't yet earn, for cloud computing Oracle hadn't built, requiring the equivalent of four nuclear plants and massive borrowing. Oracle's debt-to-equity ratio was already 500%, ten times the level for Amazon or Microsoft. The stock has since plummeted and CDS spreads have blown out from 30-50bps to over 200bps.
quote: A little over around a year ago, Oracle stopped jumped by 25 percent after they were promised 60 billion dollars a year for open AI. And what we pointed out was, well, that's the amount of money that open AI doesn't earn yet to provide cloud computing that Oracle hadn't built yet and which will require the equivalent of four nuclear plants, as well as massive borrowing by Oracle, whose debt to equity ratio was already 500 percent, which was 10 times the level for Amazon Microsoft. So we kind of felt that Oracle as a company was absurdly mispriced. And ever since then, the stock has plummeted and their credit default swap spreads have gone from, you know, 30 or 50 basis points to over 200.

headline: Dollar remains resilient despite consensus bearishness; reserve currency metrics show no material erosion
reasoning: Popular macro view has been that the dollar is overvalued given US fiscal challenges, but tracking the specific metrics that underpin reserve currency status — dollar share of FX reserves, international debt issuance, SWIFT transaction volumes, trade invoicing — shows no meaningful change. The dollar has drifted up on the year and is flat even after the Treasury intervention. Historical analysis suggests fundamentals, not interventions, drive currencies in the long run without a massive bazooka.
quote: Everybody hates it. A popular view among macro investors since trash just as the dollar is too high. Given all the problems the US faces. But you've heard me right about this. We track the specific things that make the dollar of the world's reserve currency. So the dollar share of foreign exchange reserves of international debt issuance affects transaction volumes of swift payments of trade and voicing. And we just don't see that there's enough evidence that any of those numbers are changing. And if the dollar actually drift up this year and it's still flat even after the Treasury intervention.

headline: Broad healthcare recovery validated across managed care, biotech, life sciences, pharma and services — all segments except equipment have rebounded sharply

And all segments of health care have participated except health care equipment.

headline: Earnings strength highly contingent on continued AI capex boom; growth disconnected from the broad economy
reasoning: Earnings projections are up ~10% from where they started the year, the strongest revisions year since 1996 outside of 2021. However, the share of companies with rising earnings is disconnected from the ISM manufacturing survey, suggesting growth is being driven by the boom in AI capital spending (rising from ~$200bn/year in 2024 to $750bn over the last 12 months) rather than the broad economy. Q2's ~50% earnings growth figure includes revaluation gains on Anthropic and OpenAI positions held by the hyperscalers; stripped of those, the median stock was only up 10-12%.
quote: The earnings growth appears to be very contingent on continued AI capital spending, which has risen from about $200 billion a year in 2024 to $750 billion over the last 12 months. So, generally, the share of companies with rising earnings is very closely linked to this ISM manufacturing survey. But over the last two, three years, there's a huge increase in the share of companies with positive forward EPS guidance, but not such a big increase in the manufacturing PMI. So to me, that's a clue that we're having outsized earnings growth here that's disconnected from the broad economy and very much being driven by the boom in capital spending.

headline: Chinese AI basket underperformed the US AI basket after recommendation; timing was wrong despite correct structural thesis on homegrown AI build-out
reasoning: The call highlighted 32 Chinese companies across semiconductors, software, power, electrical components, heavy equipment and interactive media building out homegrown alternatives to AI infrastructure, lithography and related supply chains. And we outlined 32 Chinese companies, semiconductors, software, power, electrical components, heavy equipped machinery, trans, you know, stuff like that, interactive media. And those stocks had done well. But as soon as we made this recommendation, they rolled over a bit and also they underperformed our US AI basket.

headline: SMRs remain unproven and likely 2-2.5x more expensive than current grid options; benchmark nuclear index has declined vs renewables and oil since March
reasoning: Even accounting for potential economies of scale, small modular reactors may cost two to two-and-a-half times more than current grid power alternatives. The concept of economically modularising and miniaturising the most capital-intensive industrial project in the world is an unproven proposition. A few tech giants may pursue SMRs as a demonstration, but as a broadly adopted grid power source, SMRs face steep proof-of-concept and proof-of-cost challenges. Since the March energy paper, the benchmark nuclear index has declined relative to both renewables and traditional oil.
quote: Even with the prospect of end of a kind cost reductions, small modular reactors might end up costing two to two and a half times more than current grid power options. And the notion that you can economically modularize and miniaturize the most capital intensive industrial project that exists in the world. It's a completely unproven proposition. A couple of tech giants might just do it to show they can do it. But as a broadly adopted form of new grid power, the SMRs face very steep proof of concept and more importantly, proof of cost challenges.

headline: Called the peak in Korean and global semiconductor stocks; hedge fund crowding, margin debt and leverage ETF risk were the warning signs
reasoning: Technical signals had breached levels not seen since the dotcom boom. Hedge fund exposure to semiconductor and hardware stocks was soaring. Korean margin debt was at extreme levels. Option premiums were elevated. Leverage semiconductor ETF market risk surged. Shortly after the June publication, Korean stock market and global semiconductors began to sell off, and stock margin loans in Taiwan, Korea, and China unwound.
quote: What spooked us was the technicals in the semiconductor stocks had breached levels that you hadn't seen since the dotcom boom. Hedge fund exposure was soaring to both semiconductor and hardware stocks. Korean margin debt was off the charts. Option premiums were flying. And then the other one that was interesting was I talked to our derivatives people. There was a surge in market risk associated with leverage semiconductor ETFs. Almost immediately after we released this piece in June, both the Korean stock market and the global semiconductors started to sell off.

headline: Missed the US small-cap recovery; small caps have outperformed large caps this year
reasoning: While the Korea and Taiwan peaks were well-called, the 2026 outlook did not highlight the possibility of a US small-cap recovery. US small cap has outperformed US large cap this year. It lives underground for 1700 years and emerges. But anyway, it emerged this year, flap its wings around and we did not highlight that opportunity.

headline: New York City mayor's property seizure policy risks repeating 1970s-80s failures; rent controls and renovation disincentives likely to reduce housing supply further
reasoning: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act made renovations deeply unprofitable for landlords, collapsing major capital investment and apartment improvement filings. Mayor Mamdani's plan to seize delinquent buildings and transfer them to nonprofits and tenant groups relies on NYC's Article 7A program, which in the 1970s-80s resulted in buildings accumulating tax arrears and remaining in deplorable condition, costing the city billions over 19 years. Rent controls, mandatory construction wage increases and property seizures are unlikely to incentivise new development and may cause some landlords to remove buildings from the market entirely to avoid expropriation risk.
quote: I don't know exactly how the Montani administration is going to avoid repeating these kinds of outcomes, without substantial taxpayer subsidies, which so far really haven't been announced... I don't understand how the new rent controls, mandatory construction wage increases and these property seizures, are going to incentivize development of new units. If anything, these policies might prompt some landlords to remove certain buildings from the market entirely given the risk of appropriation.

The company's decision to stop disclosing certain customer engagement metrics was not a confidence builder. But again, I don't understand why the stock is doing as poorly as it is.

headline: Treasury's Operation Twist likely to fail; economic strength, fiscal deterioration and hyperscaler debt crowding out Treasuries all pushing long rates higher
reasoning: The Treasury increased monthly purchases of 10-30 year Treasuries from ~$5bn to just over $10bn, but this twist is only a quarter the size of the Fed's prior operation while the stock of long-duration Treasuries has grown from $1tn to ~$6tn. Economic conditions (ISM employment, prices paid, supplier delivery indices) are all consistent with a tightening rather than easing Fed. The federal deficit is worsening in a strong economy. Hyperscaler long-duration debt issuance has surged from below $50bn/year before 2024 to ~$300bn in 2025-2026, now equivalent to ~70% of all Treasury bond issuance, crowding out buyers.
quote: The three big challenges that Besant is facing here is, number one, economic conditions are just very strong for the level of the funds rate. The second one is, obviously, everybody knows this, but the debt and the deficit number continue to deteriorate. And then maybe the biggest one that people need to spend more time thinking about is the explosion in hyperscaler debt issuance, which is crowding out the Treasury at the long end of the curve... Hyperscaler long duration debt issuance this year is 70% of all of the treasury bond issuance.

headline: Next Fed move more likely a hike than a cut; manufacturing and services price surveys inconsistent with easing
reasoning: With the exception of one cycle around the S&L crisis, the Fed almost never cuts policy rates when manufacturing and service sector price surveys are rising. Fed funds futures for December 2026 have risen almost 1% since this call was made, now pricing around 3.8%. ISM employment, prices paid, and supplier delivery indices are all at levels historically associated with Fed rate hikes, not cuts, validating the view that easing expectations were mispriced.
quote: What we wrote a year ago is that with the exception of one cycle around the S&L crisis, the Fed almost never cuts policy rates when manufacturing and service sector price surveys are rising, which is what they were doing last year. And we felt the next Fed move would be a hike rather than the niddies, despite all the pressure that that working to get from the White House. And Fed funds futures prices have risen by almost one percent for that December 26 contract since that.

headline: Chicago and Illinois have among the worst US municipal finances but credit spreads have paradoxically tightened since the bearish call, making it a wrong call on timing

They face the added challenge that most of their unfunded obligations are related to pensions, which are immutable according to state constitution... Federal stimulus money has run out and there are declining commercial property values in the Chicago loop. And those result in the largest residential property tax hikes in 30 years. The credit markets, unfortunately, show absolutely no sign of concern about this issue. And as a pie in the face to me, Chicago and Illinois credit spreads have actually tightened since we published.

headline: Hyperscaler revenue backlog surging; Google Cloud up 82%, AWS and Azure above 30%, reinforcing AI monetisation

headline: China is rapidly improving energy self-sufficiency through electrification, renewables expansion, and a 30–35% cut in oil imports, but cheap energy exports to developing nations come with a broader trade-off
reasoning: China's share of renewable final energy consumption is rising faster than anywhere else in the world. It has the second fastest pace of energy electrification after Japan. As a result, self-sufficiency reached over 80% in 2025 and has risen further in 2026 as oil imports were cut 30–35% through drawdowns of strategic reserves, coal gasification for petrochemicals, and electrification. Countries like Pakistan have benefited dramatically from cheap Chinese solar exports (solar share of electricity rising from 4% to over 20% in three years). However, Cembalest warns this energy independence dividend must be weighed against the broader flood of Chinese exports across all sectors of the economy.
quote: China has cut its oil imports by 30% to 35% through a combination of three things, drawing down on massive strategic and commercial reserves that reportedly exceeded a billion barrels at the peak. The use of gasification of domestic coal reserves to make petrochemicals instead of having to either produce or import oil and gas, they can synthetically make it by gasifying their coal reserves and then making petrochemicals and plastics from that and increase electrification.
episode_title: The Year of the Trojan Fire Horse

headline: Chinese EV export juggernaut is destroying European auto sector jobs with hundreds of thousands lost and hundreds of thousands more at risk by 2030, even as import duties fail to stem the tide
reasoning: Cembalest presents data showing China's auto export share has exploded since 2021 relative to Japan, Germany, South Korea, and the US — a chart he describes as nearly unprecedented in its shape. Europe imposed EV import duties of 17–35% on top of existing tariffs in late 2024, which caused a temporary dip but exports resumed rising. Industry associations and labour unions estimate a few hundred thousand auto jobs already lost in Europe with another 300–400 thousand at risk by 2030. The multiplier effects compound the direct job losses.
quote: The issue for Europe is a couple hundred thousand auto jobs lost so far and all the multiplier effect impacts of that with another three or four hundred thousand auto jobs at risk by 2030, according to some of the industry associations and labor unions and things like that in Europe. So there's a lot of damage that this is doing to economies that are absorbing this flood of Chinese exports.
episode_title: The Year of the Trojan Fire Horse

headline: China's state-subsidised industrial overcapacity — with 60% of new bank loans at or below prime — is the most blatant mercantilism of the post-war era and is damaging manufacturing in ASEAN, Latin America, and South Asia
reasoning: Cembalest argues China's zombie industrial firms survive prolonged negative producer prices through massive state subsidies: CSIS and OECD data show China's industrial policy spending dwarfs South Korea, Germany, Taiwan, the US, and others. The most striking metric is that nearly 60% of all new Chinese bank loans are extended at or below the prime rate of 3%, effectively providing free capital to industry. The share of Chinese industrial entities operating at a loss has doubled from 15% to 30% in recent years, yet capacity is not reduced. ASEAN countries (Malaysia, Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia) have seen manufacturing shares of GDP decline, and hundreds of thousands of jobs have been lost particularly in Indonesia and Thailand.
quote: Almost 60% of all new Chinese bank loans are actually extended at or below its prime rate of 3%. I mean, imagine if you read that 60% of all the bank loans that were being given out in the United States by the banking system were made at the Fed funds rate. Everybody would immediately borrow all tons of money. So this is the most blatant example of mercantilism in any country in the post-war era.
episode_title: The Year of the Trojan Fire Horse

headline: A global trade showdown is building as the US, Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia attempt to wall themselves off from China's unprecedented production surplus — none of which is good for China equity investors
reasoning: Cembalest draws on Logan Wright of the Rhodium Group to frame the fundamental tension: China's growth model is dependent on global demand, yet it is generating perpetual conflict with its customers. The US moved first on tariffs and duties; Europe, Latin America, and ASEAN are following. Anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations against China are proliferating. The conclusion is a looming global showdown, with the implication that China's export-led model is increasingly under threat of being walled off. This reaffirms a negative structural view on Chinese equities.
quote: We're heading for a global showdown of sorts as the US, which went first, but as the US and Europe and Latin America and Southeast Asia begin to try to wall themselves off from this massive and unprecedented production surplus in China, none of which is good news for investors in China. And we've seen the evidence of that already.
episode_title: The Year of the Trojan Fire Horse

headline: China's clean technology exports — EVs, batteries, solar — are surging on geopolitical shocks and represent a unique area of economic strength amid broader domestic malaise
reasoning: Cembalest identifies China's energy transition and export of clean technology as the standout bright spot in an otherwise imbalanced economy. China's clean tech exports (batteries, EVs, solar panels) jumped after Russia's invasion of Ukraine and again after the US invasion of Iran in 2026, each geopolitical energy shock acting as a catalyst. China is at nearly 20% EV fleet penetration — the only major car market arguably at 'escape velocity' — while all other top-10 auto markets remain below 10%. China's production capacity in solar, wind, batteries, and EVs often doubles actual production, meaning excess supply is set to flood global markets for years.
quote: China's clean technology exports, focusing for a moment just on batteries, EVs, and solar battles, they were steady in the late 2010s and then jumped after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and then jumped again earlier this year after the US invasion of Iran. So each time that you have a geopolitical event that affects oil supplies and availability and pricing, you tend to get this jump in clean technology exports.
episode_title: The Year of the Trojan Fire Horse

headline: China's structural imbalances — weak domestic demand, housing collapse, and export dependency — have delivered persistent underperformance for equity investors over 2020–2025 and year-to-date 2026
reasoning: Cembalest argues China's economic model is deeply imbalanced: soaring exports relative to weak imports, depressed retail sales, a multi-year housing collapse, and precautionary household savings rates around 45% — far above any other major economy. Despite this, near-term data (PMIs, China monitors) are not collapsing, suggesting a muddling-along scenario. The problem for investors is that muddling along is not enough — China onshore and MSCI offshore Chinese equities underperformed virtually all developed and developing markets from 2020–2025, and the trend has continued into 2026. Only India has done worse year-to-date. The structural imbalances Roach describes are not yielding equity market returns.
quote: For investors, this model that Roach described as having all these imbalances isn't really yielding any benefits to them. It may be yielding certain benefits to China, but they're certainly not yielding benefits to equity investors. China onshore and MSCI offshore Chinese equities underperformed just about everything else in the developed and developing world that we care about.
episode_title: The Year of the Trojan Fire Horse

headline: Cembalest highlights open source software's pervasive role as foundation of commercial code, creating systemic vulnerability risk across the enterprise software ecosystem
reasoning: Cembalest notes that over 90% of commercial code bases contain open source code, 77% of commercial code is made up of pre-built open source libraries, and the mean number of open source components per commercial application is nearly 1,200. With 94% of open source projects maintained by fewer than 10 developers, and 95% of vulnerabilities residing in transitive rather than direct dependencies, the attack surface for AI-driven exploitation is far larger than most organizations appreciate. He specifically names Red Hat, Databricks, GitHub, and Hugging Face as companies heavily reliant on open source.
quote: The share of commercial code bases with open source code is like in the high 90s. The share of open source projects with fewer than 10 maintainers or developers that are responsible for most of the code, 94%. And then the share of commercial code, this font is too small for me, made up of pre-built open source libraries and networks, 77%. So even within the vendor software universe, of all the things that we buy as JP Morgan, the vendor software we're buying is highly reliant on open source code. The code that we write internally is reliant on open source code. So open source code is a much bigger foundation of everything that I had ever suspected.

headline: Cembalest warns of accelerating AI-enabled zero-day cyber threats as time-to-exploit collapses from 30 days to near-zero, creating systemic risk for corporates and critical infrastructure
reasoning: Cembalest highlights that in 2020 there was a 30-day window between vulnerability disclosure and first exploitation, but that window has now collapsed to near zero. AI models are enabling attackers to both find and exploit vulnerabilities before defenders are even aware of them. The number of critical and high-severity CVEs has risen asymptotically, and 95% of Mythos vulnerability disclosures had no prior public advisory. This has significant implications for companies relying on vendor software built on open source code with up to 1,200 dependencies per commercial application.
quote: So when a vulnerability is found, it is a flaw in a piece of software that could be abused by an attacker. The exploitation process is the attacker actually abusing that software. And so typically, like if you look back several years, teams had time, you know, days between a vulnerability being discovered and an attacker weaponizing that vulnerability. Through again, you know, new tooling and in particular, various AI systems, attackers can now exploit vulnerabilities much more quickly, to the point where attackers are actually both discovering the vulnerabilities and exploiting the vulnerabilities before the defenders even know they exist.

headline: Cembalest advocates for US government-hosted domestic cyber defense strike force and targeted hardware replacement incentives for critical infrastructure to counter AI-amplified cyber threats
reasoning: Cembalest argues that private sector entities are currently left to defend themselves against state actors and sophisticated criminals, and the data suggests this is not working. He proposes a more fulsome homeland defense organization with authority to operate against adversaries within US networks, analogous to domestic law enforcement. He also floats a 'cash for clunkers'-style targeted rip-and-replace incentive for obsolete systems in critical infrastructure sectors, arguing that replacing vulnerable perimeter devices across 16 critical infrastructure sectors could dramatically reduce attacker initial access vectors.
quote: We would argue that it's appropriate for us to consider a more fulsome homeland defense organization that can actually operate against these actors within US networks. Not different than, you know, how we generally think of maybe the Department of Homeland Security or the law enforcement measures that we have that would counter criminals. Today, private sector entities are left to defend themselves against state actors, sophisticated criminals and individuals. I would argue when you look at some of the data, we're not winning. You know, the nation at large is suffering cyber attacks regularly, ransomware is a thriving ecosystem, fraud is well funded through attacks.

headline: Cembalest flags divergence between hyperscaler stock performance and semiconductor/infrastructure stocks as a potential market head-fake paralleling late-1990s communications sector dynamics
reasoning: Cembalest draws an analogy to the late 1990s when communications services stocks flatlined while infrastructure stocks continued to rise. Today, he observes hyperscalers (the front end of the AI boom) seeing stagnating stock prices and falling free cash flow, even as semiconductor, optical networking, and other infrastructure providers continue to rise. He notes this parallel warrants caution because the caboose (infrastructure) should not be going faster than the front of the engine (hyperscalers).
quote: If you look back to the late 1990s, there was a point at which the communications stocks flatlined, even though the infrastructure stocks kept on rising. And as a proxy for that, think about Juniper Networks and Verizon and things like that. So you had this period in the market where the front end, which were the communications services stocks, started to flatline, but the infrastructure stocks kept going. And it was a bit of a head fake to the market. We're having a little bit of a parallel right now because the hyperscalers, which are the front end of the AI boom, are seeing their stock prices stagnate and their free cash flow fall, even as the semiconductor and other infrastructure providers and optical networking companies are continuing to go up.

headline: Cembalest flags that only half of industrial networks are patchable, with aging OT/ICS equipment facing replacement as AI-driven vulnerability discovery accelerates
reasoning: Drawing on JP Morgan investment banking work with ABB, Honeywell, and Siemens, Cembalest notes that only slightly more than half of all industrial networks are patchable. The remainder — sensors, operational switchboards, device controllers used in air traffic control, water treatment, gas pipelines, and electricity networks — operate on 10-12+ year refresh cycles and may require full hardware replacement. This creates a potentially large capital expenditure cycle for industrial infrastructure owners.
quote: Earlier this year, JP Morgan on the investment banking side worked with some of the big industrial companies, ABB and Honeywell and Siemens. And they estimate that only a little more than half of all the industrial networks are patchable. And I spoke to them and the implication from those engineers was a lot of the rest of the equipment will eventually have to be replaced, which is expensive and I would imagine time consuming.

headline: Cembalest turns cautious on Frontier AI labs as new open and closed-weight models from Meta, xAI, and Chinese players offer comparable performance at a fraction of the cost
reasoning: Cembalest notes that the performance-to-cost frontier for AI models has shifted dramatically. New models from Meta, SpaceX's xAI (Grok), and Chinese providers now offer performance comparable to OpenAI and Anthropic's frontier models at one-third to one-tenth of the cost per task. CFOs are beginning to reconsider their token spend and may shift workloads to cheaper alternatives. This represents a serious competitive challenge to the incumbent Frontier Labs.
quote: This curve used to be such that OpenAI and Anthropik Frontier models were way better than everything else. Now you can kind of slide to the left on this chart. And Meta has a new model, SpaceX AI has a new Grok model, there's a new Chinese model, where all of a sudden you're looking at models whose performance isn't that different from the best OpenAI and Anthropik models at either a third or a tenth of the cost. And so I can imagine there's a lot of CFOs, and I've spoken to some of them already, that are starting to think about, hey, maybe these models can work for us on certain tasks, not all of them. But some of them are having a bit of a sticker shock on the token bills that they've been paying.

headline: AI-driven tech equipment and software investment has contributed more to US GDP than the rest of the economy combined for three of the last five quarters

The dollar took a 10% hit when Trump was elected, but it's been pretty stable since then. I'm not really surprised. We have this reserve currency tracker. I would expect the dollar to come under pressure if any of these metrics or some combination of them started to decline. What we look at is the dollar share of a bunch of things that are going on in the global economy like the dollar share of cross-border loans and the dollar share of international debt securities denominations and the dollar share of FX transaction volumes, of FX reserve investments by central banks, of exports invoicing, or of swift payments. As you can see in our reserve currency tracker table that we're showing, through the end of 2025, all of these metrics were pretty stable.
